displayQuote: The purpose of an organization is to enable common men to do uncommon things

meta.title: Who really said "The purpose of an organization is to enable common men to do uncommon things"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, Drucker wrote it: Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices (1973), p. 455. A reworded form, 'ordinary human beings do extraordinary things,' circulates more widely.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The purpose of an organization is to enable common men to do uncommon things'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Drucker, with a page number: Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices (Harper & Row, 1973), p. 455. It is widely recirculated in a reworded form.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Drucker wrote it in Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices, the 1973 book the Drucker Institute calls his magnum opus ↗. Wikiquote’s sourced section and LibQuotes independently place the sentence at page 455. A reworded form — “ordinary human beings to do extraordinary things” — now circulates more widely; AZQuotes credits that wording to the Routledge abridged and revised Management, p. 361, which we could not confirm against a copy.

trail: Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ lists the sentence verbatim under “MANAGEMENT: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices (1973), Part 2” at p. 455, citing the New York: Harper & Row edition.
LibQuotes ↗ gives the same page independently, as “Chapter 36, pg.455 — MANAGEMENT: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices (1973) — Part 2.”
The Drucker Institute ↗ dates the book to 1973 and describes it as the playbook for generations of executives; Wikipedia’s bibliography ↗ lists the same year and publisher.
The Internet Archive’s 874-page scan ↗ is borrow-only, and the Google Books record ↗ for the Harper & Row printing offers no preview at all — so page 455 could not be read here.
source.excerptNote: Quoted here as the 1973 text records it. Wikiquote’s sourced section and LibQuotes both place the sentence at page 455; LibQuotes adds that it falls in chapter 36 of Part 2. The Internet Archive’s scan of the book is lending-restricted, so page 455 could not be read directly for this entry.

source.rightsNote: The line comes from a book first published in 1973, so it is firmly under United States copyright — works first published in 1931 or later generally have not entered the public domain by age. Quoting one sentence with a full citation is ordinary attribution; the book itself is not free to reproduce, which is why the Internet Archive’s scan is lending-restricted.

author.name: Peter Drucker
author.heading: The man who invented management
author.bio: Peter Ferdinand Drucker was born in Vienna in 1909, fled Europe as the Nazis rose, and spent six decades in America turning management into something you could actually study. BusinessWeek called him “the man who invented management”, and his 1973 doorstop Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices became the reference book a generation of executives, nonprofit directors and civil servants kept on the desk. He died in Claremont, California, in 2005, eight days short of his ninety-sixth birthday.

misattribution.heading: Right author, drifting words
misattribution.intro: Nobody else is claiming this one — the attribution to Drucker holds up. What travels badly is the wording, and where people say it came from.

items.who: “ordinary human beings to do extraordinary things”
items.why: This is a reworded version of the same sentence, and it is now the more widely circulated one. AZQuotes serves it under Drucker’s name with the citation “Management”, p. 361, Routledge ↗ — that is the Routledge abridged and revised Management, not the 1973 book — and with a typo, “ordinary humans beings,” that has been copied onwards. We could not check p. 361 against a copy, so treat the edition as AZQuotes’ claim rather than an established one; what is certain is that the 1973 text reads “common men.”

A compressed form circulates in business commentary. Steve Denning’s Forbes essay writes that Drucker “defined the purpose of an organization as ‘making common men do uncommon things’” ↗ — and files it, along with the other Drucker lines around it, under The Practice of Management (1954). That is the wrong book: the sentence is on p. 455 of the 1973 Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices, and no page is given.

Because the line was reprinted in Drucker’s daily-reading anthology, many pages cite the anthology as the source — one such write-up ↗ quotes the sentence and credits The Daily Drucker. The anthology reprints it; the 1973 book is where it first appears.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence is Drucker’s own and it has a page number: Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices (New York: Harper & Row, 1973), p. 455 — as recorded in Wikiquote’s sourced list ↗.

context.heading: Why Drucker said it
lead: Drucker was not paying anyone a compliment. His point was arithmetic: once an organisation grows past a handful of people it gets an ordinary spread of talent, so no institution can be run on the assumption that it has hired geniuses. What separates a good organisation from a bad one, in his telling, is whether it can get uncommon results out of the perfectly ordinary people it actually has — by putting them where their strengths work and making their weaknesses irrelevant.

That is why the line sits where it does in the book. It opens Drucker’s argument about what he called the spirit of performance: morale measured by results rather than by everyone getting along, and a focus on what people can do rather than what they cannot.
detailsBody: The 1973 sentence is written in the idiom of its decade — “common men.” The version most quote sites now serve reads “ordinary human beings to do extraordinary things,” usually still tagged with the older date. The one citation anyone attaches to it is AZQuotes’, which points at “Management”, p. 361, Routledge ↗ — the abridged and revised Management, complete with a stray typo, “ordinary humans beings.” We could not confirm that page, so the rewording is best described as widely recirculated rather than pinned to a documented edition change.
context.pull: The claim is not that people are secretly extraordinary. It is that the organisation is the variable.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's sourced section for MANAGEMENT: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices (New York: Harper & Row, 1973), Part 2, lists 'The purpose of an organization is to enable common men to do uncommon things.' at p. 455.
LibQuotes cites the quote as 'Chapter 36, pg.455 - MANAGEMENT: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices (1973) - Part 2'.

AZQuotes shows the variant 'The purpose of an organization is to enable ordinary humans beings to do extraordinary things.' attributed to Peter Drucker, cited to Peter Drucker (2012), 'Management', p.361, Routledge.
This write-up quotes 'The purpose of an organization is to enable common men to do uncommon things.' and attributes the material to The Daily Drucker.

Steve Denning's Forbes essay states: 'He defined the purpose of an organization as "making common men do uncommon things."' — in a section headed '1954: Drucker's Bigger Vision Of Management' that attributes the surrounding Drucker quotations to The Practice of Management (1954), with no page cited.

The Drucker Institute gives Drucker's dates as born 19 November 1909 in Vienna and died 11 November 2005, and describes Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices (1973) as his magnum opus and 'the playbook for generations of corporate executives, nonprofit managers and government leaders'.

Wikipedia gives Drucker's dates (born 19 November 1909, Vienna; died 11 November 2005, Claremont, California) and lists the bibliography entry '1973: Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices (New York: Harper & Row)'.
The Internet Archive holds a borrowable, access-restricted 874-page scan of Drucker's Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices, catalogued as Harper & Row, New York, 1974.

Google Books lists the Harper & Row printing of Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices (Harper & Row, 1974, 839 pages) with no preview offered — the record reads 'No eBook available' and shows neither full nor snippet view.
